## Dan Ivascyn: Conviction Needs Capital


E7 • October 20, 2026


Dan Ivascyn, Group Chief Investment Officer at PIMCO, joined Morgan Stanley’s Co-President Dan Simkowitz for a deep dive on his experiences during the global financial crisis. He shared how an early underweight on mortgage-backed securities was the right call at the wrong time, and how he ultimately benefited from taking on risk as markets recovered.


**Dan Ivascyn**


We were just talking about, God, how are the rating agencies getting all this wrong? We cannot believe that they're saying that the lifetime overall losses are going to be 4-5%. That is absolute insanity. These losses are going to be 9, 10, 11, 12%. They turned out to be 30%.


**Narrator**


From Morgan Stanley, this is Hard Lessons, where iconic investors reveal the critical moments that have shaped who they are today. You'll hear about two out of consensus calls. One that was on the money and one that wasn't. Today on the show, Dan Ivascyn, Group Chief Investment Officer at PIMCO, in conversation with Dan Simkowitz, Co-President of Morgan Stanley. Ivascyn oversees one of the largest fixed income managers in the world, with $2.33 trillion in assets under management. Like many, he endured one of the hardest chapters of his career during the global financial crisis and its lead up. Here, he talks candidly about how external pressures can throw the right thesis off track, why systemic forces can obliterate a good hedge, and how conviction plus capital can equal a career-defining opportunity.


**Dan Simkowitz**


Dan, thanks for joining us.


**Dan Ivascyn**


Thanks for having me, Dan.


**Dan Simkowitz**


It's amazing, 30 years almost at PIMCO. And I've been at Morgan Stanley almost 35 years. It's so incredible how durable and important the partnership is with PIMCO. And it's been an exciting last year. We worked on some of the biggest deals in history together in the last 12 months, largely around AI infrastructure.


**Dan Ivascyn**


Yeah, I mean, it's an area of the market where there's a lot of complexity. And it's nice to get paid for complexity as opposed to economic sensitivity or, you know, credit risk in a narrow sense. So from that perspective, we're quite excited. As you know, we've worked as a team together on some deals. I'm sure there's going to be many more to come. Created a dedicated group at PIMCO. To do it right, you need a lot of different perspectives.


**Dan Simkowitz**


Yeah, I think when we worked together on the Meta data center and probably the largest deal at the time in the infrastructure space, but also in the sort of gray area of public and private credit, your team and their ability to look at it from multiple angles and be really big was really incredible.


**Dan Ivascyn**


With that said, of course, as we know, AI is going to be disruptive and increasing economy-wide productivity is one thing, companies figuring out how to make money from this technology is another. So there's some risks and you've got to be cautious, but one of the better, more scalable opportunities we've seen for clients in quite some time.


**Dan Simkowitz**


So Dan, usually on the show, we talk about an out of consensus call that worked and then another one that didn't work out so well, but usually from different eras. But I think in your context, we're going to talk about a series of calls within the same discrete time period, 2005 to 2010, which was formative for myself as I thought about markets and certainly was really important to the world of finance and to PIMCO.


**Dan Ivascyn**


Yeah, that's right. As an asset manager, you have many mistakes, many successes, but I think the ones I'd love to talk about are ones that were quite significant from a macro sense across markets and quite important from a firm perspective as well.


**Dan Simkowitz**


Let's go back to 2005. A lot of euphoria, a lot of maybe exuberance. How were you thinking about the market back then? And then tell us about the view that was forming.


**Dan Ivascyn**


Back in 2005, we were beginning to see significant innovation and more aggressive lending in the structured product areas more broadly, mostly focused on mortgages. There was a thesis that had formed around the globe, backed up by data, that US home prices on a national level never go down. They hadn't gone down too significantly over a 30-year type period. So you enter that into your model and you end up with an empirical justification to just lend more aggressively against home as an asset. So you know, myself and our team did more research here, looked at a lot of data, of course, but also got out and looked at what was going on across the industry at the time. Homebuilders, brokers, mortgage servicers, mortgage insurers, and quickly got the sense that there was a level of aggression on the lending side that wasn't sustainable and quite concerning. Even some of our own scenario analysis at the time suggested that some of the originations during 2005, and even going back to late ’04, were aggressive and not fundamentally sound. So that was the conclusion. And the recommendation and ultimately what we did to start was to get very, very defensive in that sector of the market. So, outright shorting where we could, but relative to indices or relative to our peers, significant underweights in terms of risk, which of course would perform well if there was a repricing of that risk or if there was actual realization of credit losses, but put us in a position of significant negative carry, where we were significantly underyielding our peers, even in some cases underyielding our benchmarks. So that was the starting point.


**Dan Simkowitz**


So we got called in to help the US Treasury and the Federal Reserve in the summer of ‘07. So we've got a long period between ‘04–late ’04 and ‘05 and ’07.. How does the trade progress?


**Dan Ivascyn**


Yeah, I think you may have been personally involved in some of that too, if I remember correctly. And the challenge for us was that, you know, people typically measure our performance in our industry over a three-year period, if you're lucky. As we know, the three-year period sometimes isn't long enough if you have a cycle of excess building in the system. But the bottom line is, by getting into this position early left us in a very precarious position because we were underperforming peers and underperforming peers quite significantly, because they were outyielding us for an extended period of time. So, you know, ironic. Just as people began to become concerned, we weren't so sure we could hold this position long enough. And in fact, it's quite interesting the way that these instruments work. We had been very, very cautious. We had been buying only the very safe piece that would mature, we thought, before any problems with the structural underweight, but we began to capitulate. Couldn't take it and ended up not diving back into the market, but saying, hey, look, we can't be this short for this long.


**Dan Simkowitz**


Was there a moment where the pressure really built, or a person came in, or a client said this, or a media source said, “What's going on over there?” where that capitulation started to take hold?


**Dan Ivascyn**


It was a little bit of everything. So I think there was, you know, consultant feedback, client feedback. What was amazing about the way these deals were structured is that you typically had your AAA risk, then you had the bonds beneath them that would provide protection. Typically you had a few different AAA tranches. The first tranche would get paid down, then the second tranche would get paid down, and then the last tranche, as long as there was still credit support remaining. It would mature, go away, it would fall off your system, you would have collected your yield and never saw it again. Success. So, you know, we had been conservative for years. People used to refer to the type of bonds we liked as a PIMCO bond. It was a safer bond than anyone else in the market would structure. It had very, very specific characteristics that we thought would allow our bond to mature before any problems developed. We began to capitulate a little bit at the end. So we started to buy a bigger percentage of that AAA bond. Still very safe, but just not as safe as it had been. Well, what happened was all those really, really safe bonds matured. They paid off. And then the losses came. As we ended up buying a slightly riskier AAA bond, what ended up happening is the credit support beneath us got eroded, and then the AAA started to take losses on a pro rata fashion. So that front AAA bond that used to get all the cash flow and would mature, turned into a AAA that was going to be outstanding forever, basically,


**Dan Simkowitz**


Still outstanding.


**Dan Ivascyn**


Still outstanding. So a story I tell young kids when they come in today, you can look at portfolios. Now they pay down to points where they're all minuscule in terms of the overall portfolio, but they're a constant reminder for the–and it will be the remainder of my career– about that episode and about the fact that even though you could be right for a long period of time, other pressures could lead to capitulation or a relaxation of that cautious view at, in some sense, precisely the wrong time. Because right around the corner, of course, we were proven right at the end of the day.


**Dan Simkowitz**


What's the lesson on capitulation timing and influence? I mean, would you do it differently today or is it just the reality: if it lasts long enough, you’ve got to make the move?


**Dan Ivascyn**


One lesson is that you can get the concept right, but when you're underweight risk and when a trade depends on other participants in the market changing their views, it's more unpredictable. It's just a harder, less robust trade structure in the market. The other alternative being something that structurally is very, very robust, cheap, attractive yield which creates predictability of return. Those types of investments, in contrast, just tend to be much more well-balanced, much more well-structured. So I think anytime you're underweight in the market, you need to give yourself enough time in order for the overall situation to play out.


**Dan Simkowitz**


Was size also part of it? Were you right size that you could take the duration hit or the underperformance hit, or was it both duration and magnitude and sort of out of your control market dynamics?


**Dan Ivascyn**


Yeah. So in a macro sense, we ultimately ended up doing very well with that trade across the firm. In fact, the general defensiveness ultimately worked out, and it put us in position to take risks later on as the global financial crisis played out, to make returns on the follow. That's at the firm level. Even though it worked out at the firm level, there were some mistakes structurally with that defensive mindset that occurred at the portfolio level for me. And that was the fact within some of our strategies, hedge fund strategies in particular, we were cautious. We were right on on caution, but even we didn't imagine how bad the situation would be in terms of ultimate losses. So we got creative with a trade where we said, hey, look, we're going to own the really, really safe stuff and we're going to outright short the risky tranches beneath that safe position. And that's a trade where we ultimately lost money. Quite incredible, that type of trade, under any type of reasonable scenario within the market would have worked out very, very well. It was the classic trade where you're short, but you're not paying out a lot of negative carry, you're getting your carry back and a very, very senior tranche that had never taken losses before, so made a ton of sense. Ultimately, it didn't work out.


**Dan Simkowitz**


You had a view and it was the right view around caution, but the less risky stuff just really implodes. As you've gone forward, now it's been almost 15, 16 years, how do you think about hedging and has your philosophy changed?


**Dan Ivascyn**


Oh, absolutely. I think the lesson is to your point is that there's a limit to a backtest. When there's a regime change or when things are going on that are so unusual and not captured in that historical opportunity set, in this case, this really incredible wave of aggressive lending, you have to use a different approach to analyzing risk. The second point, and probably the most important point, is related to a conversation I had with my colleague, Josh Anderson at the time. We got off work, went over to get a beer, and we were talking about losses in the mortgage area, almost chuckling and saying, God, the rating agencies are all wrong here. They look at these deals and despite the aggressive underwriting, they see 5% lifetime losses in these deals. And we said no way they're going to be much, much higher than this. They're going to be 10, even 12%, which at the time was quite out of consensus, leaning absolutely in the right direction. They turned out to be 30%. At 12%, we would have made a killing on that trade. We would have pivoted nicely to the long side. The rest would have been history. At the 30-some-odd percent, it led to considerable losses for our trade. And again, I think the lesson, you know, that I tried to take from that experience is that sometimes there's natural limitations to how outside the box you can think when you're involved or active at a sector that you grew up in where your point of reference was this historical data, how it has always been. It took merger op folks, a lot of equity traders to peer over at our market and say, oh my God, this is so ridiculous. What's going on? That loss is going to be much, much higher than even relatively cautious folks thought at the time. And I think that's quite important in this AI environment that we're in today. We know there’s massive investments in this technology. We all use it ourselves and know that this is game-changing. Something unique is going on here. But it may be hard, you know, without getting independent insights to understand just the range of potential outcomes here, especially for someone like myself that's spent 30 years in the finance industry, not in the tech space. So that was the lesson and, you know, really, really quite amazing at the end of the day.


**Dan Simkowitz**


So the equity guys came in and actually did extraordinarily well on the trade because they weren't bound by imagination. In the world we live in now, how do you grab diverse views and not repeat that lack of imagination element of the trade?


**Dan Ivascyn**


This is something I think about all the time. Over the last few years, this has not been an environment where you could just do discounted cash flow analysis, classic analysis, and expect, you know, great outcomes. Politics is driving decisions. Trade tensions, trade frictions are leading to economic results as opposed to the opposite, which used to be the case: good economy means good outcomes for politicians. Today, we live in a world where trade policy is very much focused on geopolitical tensions. There's much more conflict in the world that you have to price in. So what we try to do at PIMCO, is to leverage those perspectives. We have an outside advisory board, senior people that are willing to share their views, even if they're different than us. A lot of time on other perspectives in investment committee, above and beyond traditional financial analysis. I think appropriate humility in realizing what we’ll never be experts in, like modern technological innovation. Even from a generational perspective, this is important today. Those that are most in tune to modern technology and the resulting uncertainty or potential disruption tend to be our our newest employees, in some sense, the quietest voice within the organization. So spending a lot of time to ensure that we have as open a set of dialogue within the organization as possible, while again, having humility that we're never going to have, you know, the same perspective around this tech innovation and disruption as you're going to get up in Silicon Valley. So a lot of conversations, there, not just focusing on the bullish case, but also trying to find the bearish perspective as well.


**Dan Simkowitz**


Certainly at Morgan Stanley, the leadership today remembers third quarter of ‘07 through mid ’09 and we're still leveraging the lessons around how to manage a crisis and from our engagement with PIMCO, it certainly feels that way as well.


**Dan Ivascyn**


Oh for sure. Absolutely right.


**Dan Simkowitz**


Let's go back to fall of ‘08, pretty scary times and everybody's starting to hide. And I would say two firms really showed a lot of bravery. In your case as an investment matter in the fixed income market. And then two or three months after the bottom, Morgan Stanley agreed to buy Smith Barney. So talk me through your ability to start to re–take on risk and do analysis and deploy capital coming after such acute stress and pain in the markets.


**Dan Ivascyn**


So as you know, during this period, you needed to have the initial conditions to be able to take risk. That was a credit to us realizing and seeing some of the excesses that had developed, to be sufficiently liquid, defensive early on to be able to go on the offense. There were a lot of people that would have liked to have taken more risk, but they didn't have the liquidity. The financing wasn't always available at that time. A lot of what you needed to do was on a cash basis. And I think the same thing with Morgan Stanley were in a position to benefit from the stress of others. You don’t wish others to go through stress, but when you have the initial conditions generally right, you can then realize on the opportunity. It's interesting, as we know, there was a false rally in late ‘08. We didn't hit the bottom until early 2009. But to be able to scale a trade, you had to begin early. Timing was very, very hard, and when you were looking to react to an incredible opportunity set, you had to accept the fact that you're going to be a little bit early. You almost have to be early to be able to put on the scale of the positions, to be able to benefit clients for many, many years to come. So it was stressful along the way. Failed rallies are the worst. When people think you're finally coming out of a situation and you end up hitting new lows, that's quite detrimental from a psychological perspective. And that's exactly what we had at the time. But in retrospect, one of the best opportunities to buy at incredibly attractive prices.


**Dan Simkowitz**


So, you're in the midst of the analysis on this incredibly attractive and then ultimately incredibly successful trade. Where are the voices around fear? Whether it's a client, some of your peers... And how do you how do you engage with that, given how proximate it was to the bottom in terms of emotion, but also these false rallies?


**Dan Ivascyn**


Again, I said retrospect, it's always easier to look back on these periods than it is, you know, in the heat of the battle to make these decisions. \[It’s\] not easy to pull the trigger when when you have this massive, you know, balance sheet uncertainty across the financial industry. But we're looking at the situation. in the mortgage market and even the CMBS markets, you could buy reasonably well-structured to sometimes quite well-structured risk at dollar prices that are so low that, in a traditional sense, it's almost mathematically impossible to lose money unless someone changes the rules, basically. But it takes some convincing from an organizational perspective. You need to distill down what's a very complicated situation to someone that's got a broader role and not a specialist in the space. And to get as much buy-in as possible, because I mentioned in a traditional sense it was almost mathematically impossible to lose money. But then you start thinking about, well, what if Washington DC changes the rules? What if to support housing or to support a displaced homeowner, rules get changed? What about contract rights? All of these are low probability type scenarios that could justify these very, very low prices. And there's a lot of that news flow in the market, a lot of discussions of more extreme events. So it took a lot of filtering of the information. But I think the important point is enough odds were in our favor with a massive potential payoff, where we were able to make the decision to begin to add risk. And we're able, again, to realize on the opportunity. And it turned out to be a multi-year opportunity.


**Dan Simkowitz**


One of the things you mentioned was convincing the team, the broader team, and one of the great hedge fund investors, who's quite quantitative and analytical, says communication skills, the ability to convince people to come with you, is really critical. It sounds like on this trade, if you hadn't been able to convince the team to either do it in the size or go at all, it would have been a real disappointment.


**Dan Ivascyn**


Absolutely right. Very hard to pull the trigger when, you know, prices have gone down that much on an asset that you just didn't think it was possible. With that said, we had very trusting management. We had a process and a structure that really, really looked to leverage the ideas of the specialty teams. And there was a general sense of confidence across the platform. I'd like to think in retrospect, we did a good job communicating, but also it was to a set of additional decisionmakers across the firm that trusted us at the end of the day and were willing to yield, even though they didn't feel completely comfortable about the trade.


**Dan Simkowitz**


So you delivered incredible alpha success, organizational durability during the financial crisis. What's the hardest lesson, what's the hardest career lesson? And how have you deployed some of the lessons?


**Dan Ivascyn**


Let me start with the hardest lesson, and I'm going to go all the way back to the very beginning at PIMCO. Well, I started in 1998, right in the midst of the Asian financial crisis. We didn't have the same type of Wall Street training program. We had a little bit of training, but got dropped into the mortgage area. I did not hit the ground running. I don't know that I had the right mentorship at the time, maybe not the right support in a narrow sense, but I wasn't doing very well. So very early in my career, I was asked to potentially consider leaving the firm. Maybe not a right fit, maybe the resume looked good, but just wasn't working. I think the important lesson is that in this industry, markets can be harsh. There's good luck and there's bad luck, and you can confuse that with fundamental, you know, weakness in skillset. It's very, very confusing. Also timing matters a lot. What ultimately happened is that Scott Simon ended up joining the firm from the street, turned out to be a great mentor, I think said to folks, “Hey, wait a minute. how do you if this guy's any good? He's only been around about a year or so, going through one of the toughest market environments. He went from textbooks and pretty good grades, writing papers and doing doing math proofs, you know, to a trading desk.” Pretty tough lesson that you better be resilient in this industry. You got to accept the fact that sometimes timing is going to matter. You got to just accept failure in order to achieve ultimate success. So was the hardest lesson. I think the other point and you've mentioned this term a lot, it’s funny, even before the discussion today, I had durability written down, which is that you’re going to have highs and lows, but durability is super, super important. And you develop that through various experiences within the firm, both good and bad, different market environments. I think there's also this concept of compounding. We always talk about compounding interest, compounding returns. But I think from a career perspective there's this concept of compounding good values, good relationships, an expanded Rolodex, bringing great people into an organization, surrounding you with great people with sufficient perspectives. That's what's so important: this idea that throughout one's career, you’re expanding and compounding the support function, the relationships, Morgan Stanley/PIMCO, within our respective teams, across teams, appreciating perspectives of younger folks. So I think that's the other lesson, not a hard lesson, but a very, very important lesson in terms of success in this business.


**Dan Simkowitz**


The PIMCO/Morgan Stanley relationship and how we think of the world is exactly what you just said. It's a compounding of higher highs and higher lows. There are going to be lows in all parts of life as your professional career or your personal life, but also in the markets. And if we can build durability so you get higher highs and higher lows, it really works.


**Dan Ivascyn**


Yeah, and I probably left out the most important thing too: durability is a life concept as well. For durability, you have to have the right relationships at home, you got to have the right appreciation of playing the long game, and at times there'll be personal distractions you got to deal with. You got to have that part as right as possible. When you focus on durability, you can have a very exciting career in this business, and at the end of the day, you know, generate great outcomes for our clients.


**Dan Simkowitz**


Your lessons are amazing. I think as we take away, resiliency can drive durability, and then teamwork can drive durability. And these are a very powerful combination. Thank you. Dan.


**Dan Ivascyn**


Thanks, Dan. Absolutely.
